subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I may not have an
opportunity of speaking on this measure again and I would like to enter a very strong objection to the lightness of the burden imposed upon the heavier incomes. This tax has a very close relation to the .conscription measure, in my estimation. We must do our best to induce men to go under conscription to fight in Europe, we must put them in .as good humour as .possible and to put them in good humour we must impose a moderate tax on the wealth of this country. We cannot impose any taxation that will measure up to the sacrifice the man makes who goes to France and gives up his life or who receives wounds

that probably main him for the balance of his life. We should do our utmost to tax the people who are left at home and make them realize that they are sacrificing something. This taxation, in (my judgment, does not bring a sacrifice to any person. It should be of a character which will be a real sacrifice. The imam with $100,000 is not making any sacrifice. I would like to have $100,000 and contribute the percentage that is asked on such an income under this measure. I would be very glad to do it. I feel that the people with the smaller incomes aTe paying far more proportionately than the people with the larger incomes. The Finance Minister should aim to tax the heavier incomes until the people with those incomes realize that there is a war and that they must make a real sacrifice-something that will hurt. The President of the Patriotic Fund had a slogan'-give until it hurts.
Let the Finance Minister adopt the same principle in connection with his income tax. He says it will have to be altered when the war is over. Then, while the war is on, make the income tax something that will hurt the wealthy people of this country, and, after the war, the taxation can he altered.
I also feel very strongly that the excess profit tax should he continued, that the industries that are making large profits, especially those engaged in the manufacture of munitions or of other goods used in connection with the war, should pay heavily during the progress of the war. We need the revenue, but we also need to impress upon the men whom we are going to force to fight for us that we are making the people who are staying at home and making money out of the war bear the real burden of its cost.
Mention has Ibeen made of the Canadian Patriotic Fund. I may be wrong, hut I have believed in the voluntary system. I have always been able to go out and appeal for the Patriotic Fund on the ground that men were going to fight voluntarily and that the people at home should contribute voluntarily. I have been able to make the people in my neighbourhood see it in that light. But I am satisfied that in the next campaign for the Patriotic Fund the introduction of conscription will interfere with the raising of money by voluntary means, and I believe that the Government will eventually, if not immediately, have to raise by taxation all the money that has heretofore been raised voluntarily through the Patriotic Fund. I believe that is the
only fair method, too. It may be possible that within the next year the Finance Minister may have to devote some of the proceeds of this tax to the carrying of the work now carried on by the Patriotic Fund.
I do not mean to say that I would make the Patriotic Fund a Government undertaking; I am quite satisfied to have it operated as at present, that is, that the expenditure should be handled through the Canadian Patriotic Fund. But I should think that the money should be raised by taxation, and it may have to be raised through income taxation. For that reason we should keep in mind the necessity of making this tax as heavy as possible, at least during the war. I feel very strongly on this question because I do not want to see any men remain at home and make more money than will keep them comfortably while, other men are going away to bear the hardships of war, and possibly lose their lives.
I want to see the sacrifice as nearly as possible equal throughout the length and breadth of the country, and it cannot be an equal sacrifice until our taxation makes the people who stay at home feel that there is a war, and that they are doing something to help the men who have gone over to fight for us in Europe.

I am sorry the minister has taken that stand, because it is placing Canada in a position different from that of any country in Europe. The nations of Europe are trying to increase their population. France, which, according to Lloyd George, in an interview of two days ago, is .bearing the burden of the fight against Germany, pays a premium on families of three and four children in order to increase

the population. Lloyd George says that to-day, without France, the war would be at an end, that, great as is the sacrifice of Great Britain, it is nothing to that of France; that the spirit of the French people is the mystery of the present war. In France they encourage large families; here we do nothing. We declare by this legislation that the mere fact that the man is married, although he has no children, places him on the same footing as the man who may be called upon to rear half a dozen or a dozen children. The minister should reconsider that point. I make this appeal in the best interests of the country. Canada wants a native population in preference to a foreign population, and I think that, all things considered, we should make the married man or the married woman who assumes the responsibility of bringing up children-and we all know what a burden that is these days, with the high cost of living-is entitled to the first consideration of the state, not only for himself or herself, but for the sake of the children.

speechtext:
The House again in committee on Bill No. 117, to authorize the levying of a war tax upon certain incomes-Sir Thomas White-Mr. Rainville in the Chair.
On section 4-Income tax:

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I wish to join with those hon. members who have taken the position that subsection 1 of section 4 does not impose a sufficiently heavy rate of taxation. It has been urged as a justification for the imposition of an income tax that we are enacting a military service measure. It is said that because we are possibly to have conscription of men, we should, therefore, have conscription of wealth. That in itself is a pretty good ground for increased taxation, and I do not dispute that view as presented by hon. gentlemen this afternoon, but rather do I affirm it. There is a further reason for augmenting our revenues, and upon that ground alone this Bill is justified. We are spending in this country from $850,000 to $900,000 a day for war purposes. That will amount to something over $300,000,000 a year. The Minister of Finance informed us a few days ago that for the quarter ending June 30 of this year there was a surplus of about $37,000,000 which might be applied to war expenditures. If the balance of the fiscal year produces a similar result financially, there will be, from current revenue, a surplus of about $140,000,000 to apply to war expenditures. Our necessity in this country for a large revenue will be as great next year as this year. It will be almost as pressing five years hence as it is to-day. Therefore the maximum revenue from the present time on for a number of years will be the greatest amount that we can possibly exact from our people without doing injustice to any class. We should not model our rates of taxation under this legislation on the income tax legislation of the United States. They have barely entered the war. It is true that in their first year they contemplate an expenditure of about $11,000,000,000, and they have already increased the rates in their Income Tax Act. I anticipate	that next year	therewill be	a further	increase and
possibly the following year a still further increase. When comparing the two^ ooun-

tries we must remember that in most of the states of the Union many forms of direct taxation that we have not in this country are imposed by the Federal Government and state legislatures. With few exceptions, I think direct provincial and municipal taxation in this country is very light, and, therefore, the example of the United States is not an infallible guide for us in the circumstances prevailing in this country. We must not allow our national debt to accumulate 'any more than we can prevent, lest we have national disaster in the future and find ourselves in a .position of inability to meet the interest upon our national debt and at the same time carry on the public services of the country.
It, therefore, matters little how this legislation compares with the Income Tax Act of the United States, o:r with that of England. The question is rather: what is the utmost we can secure by taxation from the people of this country to meet our great financial necessities and augment our current revenues so as to keep down as low as possible our rapidly growing national debt? I think, therefore, the rates proposed under this measure are not sufficiently high, .and I join very heartily in the statements made this afternoon by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) on the other side of the House, the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) And other hon. gentlemen on this side. I cannot add anything to what they said this afternoon. The matter was put clearly and strongly by them. I have nothing further to say in reference to incomes under $5,000, nor as to the exemptions. When the resolution - was introduced I stated that I thought, perhaps, $2,000 was too high .an exemption in the case of unmarried men. What I really thought was that the amount .should be reduced, but I thought possibly the rate was a little high and might be made lower than 4 per cent for incomes taxable below $2,000 in amount. There .are in Canada .a great number o.f unmarried .men liable to taxation, and even if the amount of taxation is small, still the .aggregate might be very large without any great burden being imposed upon them. I have, however, nothing further to s-ay about that.
The tax on incomes of $10,000 .and upwards might very well be increased. While that m.ay impose a burden on many who will have to pay the tax, still that burden must be imposed upon some one in order to meet partially our wtar obligations. Business conditions in this country te-diay are exceptionally good; they are better than
the normal. It shall he much easier to secure a substantial amount this year, and possibly next year, than four or five years from now, and it is important that in the days of our plenty as much as possible be taken from our people to keep the Federal treasury in a healthy condition.
In the case of an income of $10,000 unmarried men and widowers without dependents are obliged to pay a tax of $400. If that were doubled to $800, do you think, Sir, that any taxpayer would object? Would it mean a very substantial additional burden on those liable to taxation under this Act? I do not think so. In the case of an income of $15,000, they have to pay $850. I do not think anybody would seriously object to paying a tax of $1,700 in such circumstances. A man with an income of $50,000 has to pay a tax of $5,300. I do not think there could 'be any valid objection if that were raised to $10,000. In the case of an income of $75,000, it is proposed to make the tax $10,000. If it were raised to $20,000 I do not think any legitimate protest would be made. It is true that in this country there are a very few people in receipt of such a large income, but there are undoubtedly some, and I think they would be content to pay a very much higher rate of taxation than is proposed by the minister. But whether they like it or not, I think they should be made to pay. I think that the rate of taxation might very well be doubled at lea^t,. on incomes of $12,000 up, if not from $10,000 up, and in many cases I think they might be. trebled.
The minister would have us Temember that very generous contributions have been made by the Canadian public to the Patriotic Fund, and that if we entrench too far upon incomes it will result in curtailing voluntary contributions to the Patriotic Fund. I submit that that is rather a weak principle upon which to .base a taxation scheme. I agree with the remarks made by the hon. member for Lethbridge this afternoon, when he suggested that hereafter the Patriotic Fund had better be sustained directly from the federal treasury. I think that from now on appeals to the public to sustain the Patriotic Fund will not meet with the response which they have met with in the past. I think it is only fair and reasonable to expect some diminution in interest on the part of the public. It is true that a great sectior of the public will contribute to this fund to the extent of their ability, but I really believe there will be serious impairment of the fund in the future if we

are to rely solely upon voluntary contributions. It is worthy, I think, of serious consideration whether or not some special tax should be imposed directly upon the people to sustain the Patriotic Fund, and to be collected by the provincial governments. It might be better still if the provinces were to take this matter up and make an annual assessment on the citizens of the province, equal to the amount collected on an average during the last three years, and pay the money over to the fund. Some room, however, should be left for those who wish to contribute voluntarily to the fund. I repeat, I do not think that payments to the Patriotic Fund should be considered when establishing a taxation scheme of this nature.
Before closing, I just wish to say a few words in reference to the business profits tax. There has apparently been some confusion in the minds of hon. gentlemen in reference to the position of the Business Profits Tax Act after the end of this year, and I should like to feel that I understood this matter thoroughly. As I understand it, the excess profits business tax is in. force for the years 1916, 1917 and 1918- and I want the minister to correct me if I am wrong-but the taxes levied come from profits of the previous year; that is, from Jhe profits of 1915, 1916 and 1917.

speechtext: My hon. friend says that the taxes are paid out of the earnings of 1915, 1916 and 1917. I say, no. Although the taxation is in respect of those earnings, it was not possible that the tax should be paid out of the earnings of 1915, because the taxation was not imposed until 1916, and most companies and firms had distributed their earnings as dividends or invested them in plant or material. In the result, by reason of this taxation being retroactive, the taxes in respect of 1915 were paid in most cases from the earnings of laid, and the taxes in respect of 1916 from the earnings of 1917, and the taxes for 1917 will be paid from the earnings of 1918, or from the accumulated earnings of this year.

speechtext: I understood the minister correctly; that is what I intended to say. For all practical purposes, the Business Profits Tax Act is in force in the years 1916, 1917 and 1918.

speechtext: Practically.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
It is true that the taxes payable in each of these years is from profits of the preceding year, but for the purposes of the revenues of the country,

the Business Profits Tax Act is in force in the years 1916, 1917 and 1918. Now the minister stated the other day that the Business Profits Tax Act expires at the end of this year, and that he does not propose renewing it, although for all practical purposes, as a revenue producing Act, it is still in force in 1918. The- last amendment to that Act imposed quite an onerous tax upon business, and may have had the effect of seriously hampering the extension of business in this country. I fear that business interests in the country will consider the minister's statement that he does not propose to renew that Act as equivalent to saying that he does not propose again to impose any tax of any nature upon business profits beyond the provisions of the Income Tax Bill. There was a great deal of objection to the last amendment to the Business Profits Tax Act, for the reason that when the minister introduced the Business Profits Tax Act he was understood to say that it would remain in force for three years, and that statement was taken as tantamount to a declaration that there would be no increase or modification of that tax.
I think it would be unfortunate to have the statement go abroad now that the principle of the Business Profits War Tax Act in, part at least is not to be renewed without that statement being accompanied by a declaration that possibly, and probably, some substitute therefore will be imposed. If in 1918 a Bill is introduced imposing taxation upon business profits, it will mee; with a great deal of opposition, and the statement now made to the effect that the Act would not be renewed will be construed as a promise that there would be no further taxation of that nature. I think that would be a very substantial objection to the statement made by the minister for some equivalent of the business profits tax after 1918. I am, of the opinion that it would be better to provide in subsection 2 of section 4, so that business people will know in the future what excess business profits tax is likely to be. It would not me operative in 1917 or 1918, except as against companies with a capitalization of less than $50,000. I ask the Minister of Finance to take this into consideration, and I submit it would be better to spend a little time now working out some scheme of the nature of the Business Profits War Tax Act as against business profits, and make it a part of this Act. Surely some taxation is in contemplation further than income tax of corporations. That is not at all substantial.

I want to say a word in regard to subsection 2 of section 4 which imposes a tax of four per cent on corporations and joint stock companies on incomes exceeding $3,000.
In the United States this particular tax has been increased, or at least a Bill has been introduced in Congress to increase it from four per cent to six per cent. I would like to suggest that this particular tax should be higher, and it should be graduated. As a matter of fact, a great number of small corporations in this country are making more money in proportion to invested capital than many of the larger corporations. There are exceptions, and of course the largest incomes are being earned by a few of the big industrial corporations. At the same time, there are scores of small corporations which are earning very large incomes and I think they might well be taxed more than four per cent on incomes in excess of $3,000. When the incomes reach $10,000, $15,000, $25,000 or more, the rate should be accordingly increased. I would like to call the minister's attention to the fact that there is no provision in this subsection in regard to taxing undistributed profits. Is there a general clause covering that later on?

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: A corporation is liable to taxation upon its profits, whether distributed or undistributed. There is a clause, which we considered for a while last night, to the effect that undistributed profits which were in the opinion of the minister being held for the purpose of evading the tax would be subject to the supertax.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I wish to repeat my opinion that the rate of corporation income tax should be increased very substantially in the larger incomes and it would be well to fix a special rate of taxation upon undistributed earnings. It is very difficult to tell when a corporation refuses to distribute its profits in order to evade the tax. It would be almost impossible, I would think, to determine this.

speechtext: I do not want to take much part in this discussion, but I would like to know if the minister will consider the insertion of a clause in. the Bill preventing big concerns which hold a great deal of property for increasing the rents on their tenants. There are many large property-holders in Montreal receiving $100,000 a year and more in rent, if they increase their rents by five per cent it will simply mean that the poor people will pay the tax. Of course, it is always the poor who pay these taxes.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: We cannot exempt landlords who derive substantial rentals from their properties. The presumption is that they are now getting all the rentals they can. maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: That is not what I mean. My point is, I would like to see a clause in the Bill prohibiting those people from raising their rents in order to reimburse themselves for the amount they have to pay as taxes un'der this Act. They are simply trying to get the tax back from the poor people.

speechtext: I think I am in a position now to deal with some matters that were suggested for my consideration before six o'clock. speechtext:
Section 4 now reads: "Unmarried persons and widows or 
widowers without dependent children." ] have an amendment to insert immediately after subsection 3 of section 4, which will be subsection 3 (a). It will be recalled that last evening the hon. gentleman from Halifax raised the question as to the husband assigning a part of his income to his wife for the purpose of evading the tax, which would be possible by reason oi the double exemption, the exemption to the wife, and the exemption to the husband. I think it well that both wife and husband should be assessed in respect of their assessable income, and should be entitled to the exemption of $3,000 each, but in order to prevent evasion of the tax, I desire to move that the following be inserted as subsection 3 (a)after subsection 3, of section 4:
A person who, after the first day of August, 1917, has reduced his income by the transfer or assignment of any real or personal, movable or immovable property to such person's wife or husband, as the case may be, or to any member of the family of such person shall, nevertheless, be liable to be taxed as if such transfer or assignment had not been made, unless the minister is satisfied that such transfer or assignment was not made for the purpose of evading the taxes imposed under this Act, or any part thereof. .
The effect of that will be that bona fide transfers, some of which might occur, will of course not be affected, but if the circumstances are such that the transfer is made for the purpose of evading the tax, in order that the benefit may be had of the double exemption, this subsection will meet the case. I understand the view of my hon. friend rather to be that the two exemptions should be allowed.

speechtext: I do not want to go back to what we were discussing, in regard to making an additional allowance for each child in the family, but I want to tell the minister that, in the United States Bill now before Congress, they make provision for $100 for each child under eighteen years of age.

hon. gentleman would pay me that compliment more often.

speechtext: The fact that the hon. leader of the Opposition agrees with it has nothing to do with the matter. I can do my own little thinking, and I do not think it is the kind of answer to give a grown-up man. I trust the minister will have a better .answer.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I did not desire
to be discourteous to my hon. friend. I just made the observation. There is a good deal to be said on both sides, and I think the Act as it stands, with exemptions to each, is probably fair. The law of the several provinces recognizes the Tight of property in the wife as an individual, and it seems to me she should be entitled to exemption.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 5-Incomes not liable to tax:

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Have you passed section 5?

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Section 5 was passed last night.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Is the minister satisfied that under paragraph (g) of section 5 a club or association, with the ingenuity, for instance, of a racing association, could not bring itself within that exemption? If the minister has given the matter thought, I would ask him for an answer. If he has not, I would commend the matter to him.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I think the word "non-profitable" would exclude such associations. It is not the intention to exempt a racing association that is operated for gain.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Racing associations would not admit they are operating for gain.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The question is one of fact. If any gain were made, they would clearly be liable under this measure. The object of this exemption is obvious on the face of it.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I was not here when section 5 was passed. I see the first exemption is "the income of the Governor General of Canada." Is His Excellency not to be taxed on his income in Canada?
Sir THOMAS W1HITE: No.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I am sorry.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I may say, so tnat there may be no misunderstanding, that this is the Government's Bill. His Excellency has nothing whatever to do with the arrangement of this Bill, nor has he been consulted in any way about it.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: His Excellency is exempt anyway. The fact that he is an Imperial officer would exempt him.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I think the exemption is a very proper one.
On section 6-Payment of tax at source:

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I assume the minister will have to make a change here to correspond with the one he made in section 4.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I was just about to do that. I beg to move:
That after the word "unmarried" in line 23 there be inserted in place of the word "men" the words "persons or widows", and that in line 22, instead of the words "two thousand" there be inserted the words "fifteen hundred".
Amendment agreed to.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
In several municipalities in New Brunswick widows are- to a certain extent exempted from taxation on their incomes or upon property owned by



them when the assessment is made upon their property. Has that fact been taken into consideration by the minister?

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I do not know that I quite understand my hon. friend. If a widow has children, she is entitled to an exemption of $3,000; if she has no children, she is entitled to an exemption of $1,500.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
She is not exempted
then by reason of the fact that she is a widow?

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Not by the fact solely that she is a widow.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Would the minister briefly state the purpose of this section and how and when it could be utilized? Could you use it for, instance in the case of brokers on an exchange?

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: This section covers a class of trustees in whom securities are vested in trust to pay over the income. It is to ensure that the Government Will get the tax from that source. We look to the trustees. Of course, if he pays it on behalf of- the beneficiary, the beneficiary is made the allowance. This is taxation at its source.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Is there anything in the Bill to cover estates? There are in this country large estates where money is accumulating, perhaps by reason of the children not being of age.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: A trustee, having property vested in him and having an income in respect of it, is liable to pay. If he pays, in respect of the share of income which the beneficiary receives, the beneficiary receives credit for that payment; but if, under the conditions of the trust under which he is acting, he gets income which he accumulates for those who may come into being, say' a generation from now, he i-s liable as a person in respect of that income, so that the estate is taxed.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: That is the case of a "trustee" estate, but there are many estates which are not "trustee" estates. Suppose a man makes a will and he appoints an ordinary executor.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I was considering him as a trustee.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
If the minister considers him as a trustee possibly the Bill covers that case.
Section as amended agreed to.
[Mr. Michaud. J
On section 7-Annual returns to minister of total income:

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Are special forms to be sent to the taxpayers?

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
There are certain forms in the schedule, but we have power given under a later provision of the Bill to call for such information as we require from the taxpayer, and the mode of administration will be just as under the business profits-tax, to -send the necessary forms to citizens and to have them filled in and returned to the department.
Last night the hon. member for Rouville took exception to the word " suspected " in line 9, on page 6. It is a rather obnoxious word, although it has an apt meaning. Out of deference to my hon. friend's objection, I beg to move that the word " suspected," in subsection 2 of section 7, be struck out and the word " believed " substituted therefor.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 8-Additional information.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Subsection 2 gives the .minister power to require " the production, or the production on oath." Why this difference? Is it not sufficient to have simply 'the words " the production?"

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I think it is well that we should have the power to compel the production of these documents bn oath, but, of course, the .power should be exercised wisely. Suppose that you are not satisfied with the statement a citizen has made. It is an extreme case, but it is well that power should exist to make him make the statement under oath.
Section 'agreed to.
On section 9-Penalty.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: By the preceding section the minister may compel a man to produce letters, accounts, etc., on oath. Subsection 2 of section 9 says that " any person making a false statement " shall be liable on summary .conviction to a certain penalty. Now, if a man makes a false statement under oath he is guilty of perjury, and he ought to have the benefit of a jury, and not be tried .simply by a magistrate.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I think he would be liable to both. If a man commits perjury he would be liable under the Criminal Code. The provision in subsection 2 of section 9 for .a penalty on summary conviction

is ito addition to the penalties of the Criminal Code.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Under subsection 2 he would be liable to 6 months' imprisonment, and he could still be brought before a high court.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: A man should not be subject to two trials and two penalties. It should be either the one or the other. It is all right to provide for a penalty on summary conviction, but if a man makes a false statement under oath he ought to be tried by jury.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I think it is very desirable that power should exist to ask for a sworn statement.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Possibly.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
If he made a
false statement in the returns he would be liable to the penalties provided here, and I think he could be proceeded against for perjury.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
The lawyers
will have to disentangle it.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I do not think
any particular harm will be done bv retainr ing this provision.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I call the minister's attention to what seems to me to be a hardship. In line 26 of page 6 it is provided that:
Such returns shall he delivered to the minister on or before the twenty-eighth day of February in each year, without any notice or demand being made therefor.
Then section 9 provides for a penalty of $100 for each day during which the default continues. Now firms or individuals may unknowingly default.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Legislation of
this kind always runs this way. There is confidence that the Government will not exercise the powers given here oppressively, in the case of a citizen defaulting unknowingly. It is necessary that the onus be put on the citizen of making the returns. But in the practical working out of the Act, just as in the Business Profits Tax Act, the various officials throughout the country will send the forms out and keep in touch with the recipients until the returns are made. 1 think I can assure my hon. friend that no such injustice as he imagines may result will be done to citizens.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The word "shall' is imperative, and looks very severe indeed.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
As my hon. friend knows, it is a penalty not exceeding $10,000. 262i
There is always discretion within the limits fixed. It might be a fine of $10 or $50.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Ignorance of the law is no excuse, but how is an ordinary citizen, who does not read our deliberations and who does not get the statutes, to know that he must make his returns before February 28th?

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: We will contrive to let him know. We will get the organization, and secure information as to the citizens thought to be liable, give them the forms, and have these forms filled in. I admit it is a big task.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: What organization has my hon. friend in mind?

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: At the present time we have the business profits war tax organization. We have a Commissioner of Taxation, an assistant commissioner, and a staff in the Finance Department. Then we have representatives in every province from Nova Scotia to British Columbia. That organization can be extended by the addition of other officials. We have the province of Ontario divided into districts, with, I think, four men in charge. They have stenographers and such other assistants as are necessary. The whole Dominion is covered, and by the expansion of that staff the business profits taxation assessment could be made, and this taxation as well.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: There is a good deal of force in what was stated by my hon. friend from Huntingdon (Mr. Robb). Men in the country may forget they are assessable. Will your officers look after the assessment rolls in every municipality, and search out the parties who are likely to he assessable?

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: We shall be obliged to do it. We would not expect to administer this tax upon the unsolicited returns of the public. It would not be possible to do it. The country will have to be covered. It will have to be ascertained, so far as it can be, who are properly liable to assessment, and those persons will be notified, just as the assessment department here notified taxpayers. It will take some time to get the system under way, and the organization will be more or less imperfect for a while. It took three or four years to get the United States organization working properly.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Does not the minister think it would be better to impose a smaller penalty, and collect it as a tax? Give the

people proper notice, and if they fail to *comply with it put on a small tax, and collect it. One hundred dollars' a day might be more than the tax would amount to. The penalty might be greater than the . tax. Under the Massachusetts law the penalty is five dollars for each day a person is in default. That looks like a reasonable figure, and it might be collected.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I am quite satisfied from my experience in office that nobody will be harmed through the infliction of penalties. I think it is desirable that there should be legislation in regard to penalties, so that citizens may be compelled to make the returns called for. I do not think it is necessary to reduce the penalty. I am quite sure no! hardship will result. It is a sanction to the Act.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: If the fine is not paid, what will happen? Will a distress warrant issue, or how will the amount be collected?

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
There is provision later pn for collection. It is a debt owing to the Crown, and is covered by section 20, which says:
The taxes and all interest and costs assessed or imposed under the provisions of this Act shall be recoverable as a debt due to His Majesty from the person on whom it is assessed or imposed.

Section agreed to.
On section 10-Assessment:

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Does the minister not think it would be fairer if the tax were payable within thirty days from receipt of the notice, instead of thirty days from mailing of the notice?
Sir THOMAS WHITE; That brings up a difficult question. You can prove when a notice is mailed, but it is hard to prove when it is received.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
The notice would be
sent by registered mail.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
It is hard to
know, from the department's standpoint, when it is received. Of course, a citizen will be allowed a certain leeway.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
There might be instances
where men would be travelling and would not receive their notices.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I can assure my
hon. friend that there will mot be any harsh exercise of the powers given under the Act.

Section agreed to.

On section 12-Board of Referees:

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
What is the duty of
these referees?

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Section 13 defines them.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: How many of these boards will you have and will they be distributed over the country?

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: That would depend on the number of appeals. From our experience of the Business Profits War Tax Act I should say that it would not be necessary to appoint permanent boards but if there should be a number of appeals in, say, Nova Scotia, we would appoint a *board of referees consisting of one, two or three member's for the purpose of hearing and determining appeals. There may be very few appeals and there would be no use in appointing a permanent board in each province because that would involve considerable expense. We might appoint a county judge, or some lawyer of standing, or a business man, as the case might be, have a court of revision held and havte the appeals disposed of in a summary fashion.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: What remuneration is provided for these referees?

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: There is no remuneration fixed in the Act. It would be a matter of arrangement like the appointment of a commission under the Inquiries Act. I am told by the parliamentary counsel that it is no't necessary to insert in the Act the amount of remuneration. It would only hamper us in the administration of the Act to do so-. I should say that the usual fee of $20, $25 or $30 a day for a lawyer or county judge acting as a referee would be paid, but I should not like to be confined to that. At all events, we have not any large amount in view if that is in the mind of my hon. friend from Huntingdon (Mr. Robb).

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The only advantage of having local referees would be that the appeal would be brought to the domicile of the taxpayer; otherwise it would be better to send it to the court at once.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Precisely.
On section 13-Court of Revision:

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Does the minister propose to provide any machinery by which parties will have notice of their rights under this Act? People generally will never see this Act. When a man gets notice of

his assessment he should at the same time get notice that he is entitled to appeal because otherwise he would not know anything about it. There should he forms sent out by the minister which should contain notice that the party assessed is entitled to appeal.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Surely. My hon. friend is aware that on an ordinary assessment slip sent out there is at the foot, or on the back, or in some conspicuous place, a notice that parties desiring to appeal must make a return within a certain time. If my hon. friend will look .at the schedule, he will see that a form is provided, of a very simple character, on which a man is entitled to give notice of appeal against the assessment on the ground that he has been wrongfully .assessed. There is nothing technical about it.

Section agreed to.
On section 15-Hearing and decision by board:
iMr. ROBB: Does paragraph one of this section mean that the board has only the right to increase assessments?

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The board shall determine the matter. The matter will be the matter of the appeal. The taxpayer will be appealing on the ground that he is wrongfully assessed and it will be for the court to reduce or confirm the assessment. Then the power is given, if the court thinks it is a proper case, to raise the assessment. It is the same power that is exercised by the ordinary court of revision in regard to the assessment of real property.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Should it not read:	"May
increase or decrease the assessment"?

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I submit that the section as it appears is necessary for this reason:	The appeal will be on the ground
Nthat the assessment is too high or that the assessment should not have been made. In determining the matter, it is clear that the board may reduce the assessment or hold that the party is not liable for it. The appeal will not be on the ground that the as-[DOT] sesament should be increased. Therefore we think it necessary to provide that the court shall increase the assessment.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I think we
should not use such power as that. The minister has power to increase the assess^ ment himself. The poor taxpayer, who thinks he has been assessed too heavily, appeals to the board and the board should simply have the power to determine whether he has been assessed too heavily or not. It should not go beyond that. If he is not taxed sufficiently, it is for the minister to look after that and not for the board.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
It is extraordinary how often I find myself in agreement with my right hon. friend but I do not on this occasion. This is to be the law. If a party comes before the court and it appears that a mistake has been made, that he has not been assessed enough, he submits himself to the jurisdiction of the court and if the court says that his assessment shall toe increased, it will only be because he is liable for an increased amount.
It is by no means an unusual provision, in fact I think there is a similar provision in many Assessment Acts. It is very seldom exercised, but I think it should be there because the purpose of the court is to see that a proper assessment is made. No hardship can result to the man in question, because the assessment depends upon his return, and if the court should find that he is assessable for more than the amount for which he has been assessed, it only means that he has not made a proper return. So, while in minor matters I usually agree with my hon. friend, I do not find myself agreeing with him to-night.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I have been brought up under a system, that of the civil code, under which the court cannot go beyond the prayer of the suitor. I think that is a very sound principle.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I agree that if the assessment is not regarded as sufficient the department should have the right to appeal, that either party should have that right. I find no provision for the Crown to appeal. The man who is appealing is the party assessed. He comes before the court prepared to sustain his petition, but how is he to meet the case of an increased assessment sprung upon him there?

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: My hon. friend has been a judge, and I have no doubt a very just judge. What hardship would likely arise if my hon. friend, sitting as a court of revision, should find that the man had not made a proper return and was assessable on a larger income than he had stated, either inadvertently or otherwise? That power is vested in the court, it will be observed.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I wish to call attention to section 8, which empowers the minister to ask for more information. The ratepayer has made his return to the min-

ister, and the minister may ask for more information. But here you are saying that the court shall have power to say to the man: You are not assessed fully. I say that is not what should be contemplated by the law. The appeal should be made and the prayer should be heard and decided only upon the complaint of the taxpayer that he is taxed too heavily.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I cannot appreciate the point of view of my right honourable friend. If, in the course of the suitor's evidence, it transpires, under the questioning of the court, that his income, instead of being $5,000, is $20,000, the court says: Not only have you no cause for complaint, but it is clear that under this measure you should be assessed for $20,000. It is most unlikely that any injustice would result from placing this power in the hands of the court.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I do not agree with my hon. friend's practice. If, for instance, au appeal is made against an assessment of' $20,000, then the issue is whether $20,000 is the right amount. The position of the department in the court will be to sustain that $20,000 is right. The issue will not permit the minister to show that the assessment should be $30,000 instead of $20,000.
That issue will not allow him to do that. He can sustain what he was done, and the other man's position is to controvert that. But in supporting his assessment of $20,000 he will not be permitted to get an assessment of $30,000. That is a clear cut issue that will be before the court, and the court must stand by the issue.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
In Nova Scotia we have an Act on the statute book for many years which has worked successfully, and just exactly the same powers are given to an Assessment Appeal court in that Act as are proposed under this Act. The Assessment Appeal court has the power to increase the assessment, even though the appeal be made to have the assessment decreased. Having acted in the capacity of a member of the Appeal Court, I find it works very well, because the ratepayer who thinks he is aggrieved must exercise his judgment before taking an appeal. These appeals are made in a frivolous manner sometimes, but if the person who feels himself aggrieved knows there is not only a chance of his assessment being decreased, but a possibility of it being increased, he exercises more care. That provision prevents frivolous appeals. It has worked out very well

in Nova Scotia, and I think in nearly all the provinces that have a similar Act.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I am quite familiar
with the provision in the Act to which the hon. gentleman from Annapolis refers. That provision has been in our Act for ma,ny years, but I do not know of any cases where it was acted upon but one, and that was last winter, in the case of some milling concern in the neighbourhood of where my hon. friend lives, and there was the greatest possible row about it. They undertook, of their own motion, according to the language of our Act, to increase the assessment, without dealing with it under proper notice of appeal, and giving notice to the other side. It came up before our Supreme Court, and such men as Mr. Justice Harris decided it was absolutely wrong to use such powers in that way. Mr. Justice Bitchie agreed with him, and it was a divided court, but two such men as Mr. Justice Bitchie and Mr. Justice Harris said such power should never be used, that ample notice should be given to any litigant of any application to have his taxes increased, and the count should not act of its own motion, although the provision happened to be in the Act. I think the hon. gentleman from Annapolis will find that was the only time, in the history of Nova Scotia, 'that it was ' acted upon without proper notice being given to the other side that it was the intention to increase or decrease, as the case may be.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman is in error with reference to that. He alludes to the case of the municipality of Annapolis versus the Davidson Lumber Company. In that case, when the Assessment Appeal Court Tai-sed the assessment, it was on the appeal of a ratepayer, and not upon the appeal of the owner of the property. There are very, very many oases in the county of Annapolis, 'and in cither parts of the province, which have come under my observation where the assessment court rtaised the assessment, although the appellant had asked for a decrease.

Section agreed to.
On section 2, subsection (f)-Definition taxpayer.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
My right hon. friend asked that this section be allowed to stand. I think we might pass it now. I desire to amend this section by changing

the word " suspected " to the word " believed."

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Section 15 provides for costs. I suppose as a rule the men who will be litigating here will be so wealthy that costs will not bother them very much, but some litigants will not' be wealthy, and the question of costs will be important to them. I find that the minister in section 15 adopts as the scale of fees the tariff of fees in force in the Exchequer Court of Canada. If a man who has only a small amount at stake-the amount may not be very large, but it may be important to him -is thinking about appealing, and he knows there may be a counsel fee of $200 taxed against him, he may not feel that he is in a position to appeal. The scale of fees in the Exchequer Court is the highest in any court of Canada, and I do not quite see why this question of costs should not be left 'entirely in the discretion of the board which could fix a lump sum that would be commensurate with the proceedings. If the board has to say: You are entitled to costs, then they have no discretion but to allow the scale of fees prescribed by the Exchequer Court. This court of appeal should be a simple court, not restricted by any close or hard rules of practice. A lawyer should not be necessary. People should be able to go before this board without any formality, just as they do before the Railway Board. If the Exchequer Court fees prevail, and an appellant is up against a taxing master who will under this scale of fees tax the cost at $300 or $400, when the matter at stake is very much less than that, a man who may have a grievance will be afraid of risking the possibility of being mulcted to that extent.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend. I know from experience that costs are taxed fairly high in the Exchequer Court, and under this measure a man should be given an opportunity of appearing before an appeal board without having to pay too heavy costs.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
The suggestion is a very good one. The court should be one in which the fees are reasonable, especially as the appeal will be against the Crown. I beg to move that section 15 be reconsidered.
Motion agreed, to.
On section 15-Hearing and decision by board:

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I beg to move:
That the last sentence of subsection 2, be struck out and the following substituted therefor :
The costs shall be as may be prescribed by the Board.
~ Mr. A. K. MACLEAN: Why not say: "The tariff of fees"?

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Very well. Make it read: "The tariff of fees shall be as prescribed by the board."

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: If the board does not order any costs, there will be no costs.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The costs will be absolutely in the discretion of the board.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: A man may succeed in his appeal and the board may, in rendering judgment, not assess the costs, and he will have to pay his own costs.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
The Board is a
judicial body and the costs are in the discretion of the hoard, but the discretion should be a reasonable one and, I have no doubt, would be. I do not see how we could divest the board of discretion as to costs.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Then there will be no
tariff; the fees are discretionary.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The costs are discretionary.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: As the subsection stands, the costs are as in the Exchequer Court. There you have a fixed tariff. Under this amendment you niay have any tariff.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
It has been
pointed out that the Exchequer Court fees are higher than the ordinary court fees.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: No, lower.

maintopic: WAR TAX UPON INCOMES. CONSIDERATION OF BILD IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: They are lower than the ordinary court fees in Quebec, but not lower than the ordinary court fees in Nova Scotia. The costs might be fixed by the board, and probably they would have regard to the tariff in force in the several provinces, because we shall appoint a board to deal with Nova Scotia appeals and one to deal with Quebec appeals. On the whole I think the amendment makes the matter fairly satisfactory.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
